title: rollback-oscillation-hierarchical-rollout-postmortem
summary: During a staged hierarchical rollout of v2 model weights to US-West and EU regions, automatic rollback automation began flipping the traffic split repeatedly between the old and new model variants (oscillation). This caused intermittent 5xx errors and increased tail latency for chat paths that use long context. The automation toggled ~6 times over a 40-minute window before manual intervention stabilized traffic. User-facing impact included degraded response times and ~0.8% error rate increase for affected routes. Root causes: a model-mapping config drift across regions combined with a rollout-controller race condition and overly-sensitive rollback heuristics.
timeline:
2024-11-18 09:12 UTC - Canary starts in us-west small traffic (5%).
2024-11-18 09:25 UTC - Canary healthcheck shows elevated error rate for long-context chat requests (~1.5% in window). Automatic rollback triggers: controller reduces traffic to 0%.
2024-11-18 09:28 UTC - Controller re-applies rollout to try again (bug in backoff logic), pushes traffic to 5% once more.
2024-11-18 09:31 UTC - Error rate spikes again; rollback triggers. Repeat toggles observed ~09:25-10:05 UTC.
2024-11-18 09:44 UTC - SRE on-call manually disables auto-rollback policy and pins canary to 0% pending analysis.
2024-11-18 10:05 UTC - Investigation identifies inconsistent model_map metadata between regions (us-west had model_map_v2 flag true; eu had stale model_map_v1).
2024-11-18 11:20 UTC - Manual rollout with verification steps (manifest etag checks) applied; canary resumed and gradually increased with no further oscillation.
2024-11-18 12:40 UTC - Incident declared resolved; follow-ups tracked in JIRA-OPS-1284.
root_cause:
Primary: A config drift where the model_map mapping used by the rollout-controller contained region-specific entries that were not synchronized. us-west had a mapping that pointed some microroutes to a quantized variant of the model while EU was still pointing to the v1 baseline. The rollout-controller's pre-flight checksum validation only ran locally and did not verify cross-region parity, so the canary saw mixed model behavior when traffic was routed across region-aware backends.
Secondary: The rollback automation lacked sufficient hysteresis/backoff. A bug in the rollout-controller's backoff algorithm caused it to re-attempt the same canary step immediately after rollback instead of waiting longer, creating a flip-flop. Health-check thresholds were tuned for short windows and were overly sensitive to long-context tails (the failure mode only manifested on sequences >4k tokens).
mitigations:
1) Immediate: Disable automatic rollback for the rollout job and pin traffic to stable variant until manual verification.
2) Deploy a hotfix to the rollout-controller to enforce exponential backoff after a rollback (github PR #371).
3) Publish a temporary admission check in the control-plane to block rollouts when model_map metadata etags differ across target regions.
4) Reverted recent config changes to model_map staging propagation that had introduced a one-hour async propagation window.
postmortem_analysis:
- The error signature: increased decoder stalls and occasional OOM traces on a small subset of workers that had been assigned the quantized weights without the matching runtime flag, causing rare incompatibility with the KV cache layout. Logs showed 'kv_cache: shape mismatch' in ~0.4% of failed requests.
- Monitoring gaps: There was no cross-region consistency monitor for model_map/manifest etags. The rollout-controller only reported local checksum mismatches as warnings, not blockers.
- Runbook gap: The canary rollback runbook assumes single-source-of-truth mapping and did not require a manifest-etag parity check before enabling auto-rollback.
- Human factors: On-call saw repeated alerts; the controller's toggling generated alert fatigue and delayed manual diagnosis.
follow_up_actions:
1) Add a 'manifest-etag parity' pre-flight check in rollout-controller (owner: eng-platform, ETA: 2024-12-08, tracked in JIRA-OPS-1284).
2) Change auto-rollback policy defaults to include backoff and 3 consecutive windows before a rollback is triggered; update runbook and default SLO thresholds (owner: eng-sre, ETA: 2024-12-01).
3) Create a cross-region monitor (grafana alert) that fires when model_map etags diverge between any two active regions for the same deployment (owner: observability, ETA: 2024-12-05).
4) Add an integration test in CI that simulates staggered model_map propagation and asserts the controller blocks the rollout until parity is reached (owner: release-engineering, ETA: 2024-12-15).
5) Training: schedule a runbook walkthrough and tabletop exercise for rollout oscillation (owner: SRE leads, date: 2025-01-10).
runbook_changes:
- New pre-flight step: verify model manifest etag parity across target regions.
- New rollback policy: require 3 failing windows across at least 2 independent samplings OR sustained errors for 10 minutes before auto-rollback.
- Add 'mute controller toggles' switch to on-call UI so humans can pause automated re-tries without redeploying.
- Update healthcheck probes to include long-context synthetic traces for routes that are sensitive to sequence length.
metrics_and_impact:
- Affected routes: /chat/respond and /chat/stream (long context).
- Peak error delta: +0.82% 5xx above baseline during oscillation window.
- Traffic impacted: approx 7% of total global chat traffic was subject to the canary at any given toggle.
- Duration: 40 minutes of oscillation, ~3 hours until full verified rollout completion.
- Customer-visible complaints: one internal customer reported timeouts on an experimental feature; no production SLA breaches recorded.
lessons_learned:
- Cross-region state must be treated as a single source of truth for staged rollouts; local-only checks are insufficient.
- Automation is powerful but must include conservative hysteresis and clear human override paths.
- Synthetic long-context health checks are necessary for model changes that affect attention/kv cache paths.
- Small metadata propagation delays can have outsized operational effects when combined with aggressive auto-remediation.
